related.note: だけ is the base 'only/just'; だけは adds the sense of a singled-out, guaranteed minimum.
限り marks 'as much as / to the limit of' (できる限り); it overlaps with the やれるだけ effort sense of だけは.

title: だけましだ
meaning: at least ~ is better; it could have been worse
summary: だけましだ says that although the situation is bad, it could have been worse, so one saving grace makes it 'at least better than nothing'. まし means 'the lesser evil', so the tone is resigned relief rather than genuine satisfaction.
structure: Verb・い-adjective［plain form］ ＋ だけましだ
Noun ＋ な ＋ だけましだ
pitfalls: まし means 'the lesser evil', so the overall situation is still unwelcome — this is relief that things aren't worse, not real praise.

examples.ja: 給料は安いが、残業がないだけましだ。
examples.en: The pay is low, but at least there's no overtime, so it could be worse.
examples.f: ｜給料[きゅうりょう]は｜安[やす]いが、｜残業[ざんぎょう]がないだけましだ。

examples.ja: 電車は遅れたが、座れただけましだった。
examples.en: The train was late, but at least I could sit down, so it wasn't so bad.
examples.f: ｜電車[でんしゃ]は｜遅[おく]れたが、｜座[すわ]れただけましだった。

synonyms.note: ほうがましだ compares two bad options and picks the less bad; だけましだ finds a redeeming point within one situation.

related.note: せめて wishes for a bare minimum; だけましだ accepts a small consolation already gained.

title: た末に・の末に
romaji: ta sue ni / no sue ni
meaning: after (much) ~; finally, at the end of
summary: 末に marks a long or difficult process that finally leads to a result — 'after much ~, in the end...'. It stresses that the outcome came only after considerable effort, hesitation, or hardship. The result may be good or bad, but the focus is the drawn-out road to it.
pitfalls: Use the た-form for verbs (悩んだ末に) and の for nouns (議論の末に).
It stresses a result reached after a prolonged process; for a simple sequence 'after doing', use 〜てから instead.

examples.ja: さんざん迷った末に、留学することを決めた。
examples.en: After endless hesitation, I finally decided to study abroad.
examples.f: さんざん｜迷[まよ]った｜末[すえ]に、｜留学[りゅうがく]することを｜決[き]めた。

examples.ja: 長い議論の末に、計画は中止と決まった。
examples.en: After lengthy discussion, it was decided in the end that the plan would be scrapped.
examples.f: ｜長[なが]い｜議論[ぎろん]の｜末[すえ]に、｜計画[けいかく]は｜中止[ちゅうし]と｜決[き]まった。

synonyms.note: あげく also means 'in the end after ~', but almost always leads to a bad or unwanted outcome; 末に is neutral.

related.note: 結果 focuses on the outcome '(as) a result of'; 末に stresses the long process that led there.

title: たちまち
meaning: instantly; in no time; in a flash
summary: たちまち is an adverb meaning that something happens with great speed, almost at once — a change completes 'in no time'. It often describes a sudden, sometimes striking shift affecting a whole situation, and feels more vivid and literary than すぐ.
pitfalls: It describes how fast a change unfolds; it does not mark the point in time 'the moment that ~' — for that, use とたん(に).

examples.ja: 新商品はたちまち売り切れてしまった。
examples.en: The new product sold out in no time.
examples.f: ｜新[しん]｜商品[しょうひん]はたちまち｜売り切[うりき]れてしまった。

examples.ja: 火はたちまち建物全体に広がった。
examples.en: The fire spread through the entire building in an instant.
examples.f: ｜火[ひ]はたちまち｜建物[たてもの]｜全体[ぜんたい]に｜広[ひろ]がった。

related.note: たとたん(に) marks the exact moment one thing triggers another; たちまち describes the rapid speed of a change.

title: たった(の)
meaning: only; just; a mere
summary: たった emphasizes that a quantity is surprisingly small — 'only this much, a mere ~'. The optional の comes before the number (たったの千円). It stresses that the amount falls short of expectation, often with disappointment or to underline how little there is.
pitfalls: たった attaches to a specific amount or number to stress its smallness; it is not a general 'only' like だけ that can follow any noun.

examples.ja: この会社はたった二年で全国に店を広げた。
examples.en: This company expanded its stores nationwide in a mere two years.
examples.f: この｜会社[かいしゃ]はたった｜二[に]｜年[ねん]で｜全国[ぜんこく]に｜店[みせ]を｜広[ひろ]げた。

examples.ja: 財布にはたったの五百円しか残っていなかった。
examples.en: I had a mere 500 yen left in my wallet.
examples.f: ｜財布[さいふ]にはたったの｜五[ご]｜百[ひゃく]｜円[えん]しか｜残[のこ]っていなかった。

synonyms.note: だけ is a neutral 'only'; たった adds emphatic surprise at how small the amount is.
のみ is a formal 'only' without the emotional stress; たった dramatizes the smallness.

related.note: ばかり with a number gives an approximate amount ('about'); たった pins down an exact, strikingly small figure.

title: たまえ
meaning: do ~ (mild command from a superior to a subordinate)
summary: たまえ attaches to the ます-stem to give a gentle order from someone of higher standing to someone below — a boss to a subordinate, a teacher to a student. It sounds masculine, somewhat old-fashioned and literary, and softer than a blunt imperative. It is rare in everyday modern speech.
pitfalls: Attach it to the stem: 座りたまえ, not 座るたまえ.
It presumes the speaker outranks the listener and has a dated, masculine flavor; it is not a neutral polite request.

examples.ja: まあ、そう慌てずに、まず座りたまえ。
examples.en: Now, don't be in such a rush — have a seat first.
examples.f: まあ、そう｜慌[あわ]てずに、まず｜座[すわ]りたまえ。

examples.ja: 用が済んだら、すぐに知らせたまえ。
examples.en: Once you're finished, let me know right away.
examples.f: ｜用[よう]が｜済[す]んだら、すぐに｜知[し]らせたまえ。

synonyms.note: なさい is a firm command often used parent-to-child; たまえ is masculine, superior-to-subordinate, and more dated.

related.note: 命令形 is the blunt imperative like しろ/来い; たまえ is a gentler, more refined order.

title: ちっとも〜ない
meaning: not at all; not in the least
summary: ちっとも pairs with a negative to stress 'not even a little' — a colloquial, emphatic way to deny something completely. 少しも and 全然 are close in meaning; ちっとも sounds the most casual and conversational of them.
structure: ちっとも ＋ … ＋ ない ［negative predicate］
pitfalls: It requires a negative predicate; ちっとも with an affirmative is ungrammatical.
It is colloquial — in formal writing, 少しも or 全く fits better.

examples.ja: 一生懸命練習しているのに、ちっとも上手にならない。
examples.en: Even though I practice hard, I'm not getting any better at all.
examples.f: ｜一生懸命[いっしょうけんめい]｜練習[れんしゅう]しているのに、ちっとも｜上手[じょうず]にならない。

examples.ja: 彼は謝るどころか、ちっとも悪いと思っていない。
examples.en: Far from apologizing, he doesn't feel he's in the wrong in the slightest.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜謝[あやま]るどころか、ちっとも｜悪[わる]いと｜思[おも]っていない。

synonyms.note: 全く〜ない is a more emphatic 'not at all' usable in writing; ちっとも is casual and conversational.
決して〜ない is a firm 'never, by no means' (often a resolve or refusal); ちっとも simply denies any degree.

title: ちなみに
meaning: by the way; incidentally; for your information
summary: ちなみに introduces a related piece of supplementary information the speaker adds to what was just said — 'incidentally, for reference...'. Unlike a topic change, the added detail stays connected to the current subject, offering a useful aside.
pitfalls: The follow-up should be related side information; to switch to a genuinely new topic, use ところで instead.

examples.ja: この資料は無料で配っています。ちなみに、英語版もございます。
examples.en: We're handing out these materials for free. Incidentally, an English version is also available.
examples.f: この｜資料[しりょう]は｜無料[むりょう]で｜配[くば]っています。ちなみに、｜英語[えいご]｜版[ばん]もございます。

examples.ja: 会議は午後からです。ちなみに、場所は先週と同じ部屋です。
examples.en: The meeting is in the afternoon. For your information, the venue is the same room as last week.
examples.f: ｜会議[かいぎ]は｜午後[ごご]からです。ちなみに、｜場所[ばしょ]は｜先週[せんしゅう]と｜同[おな]じ｜部屋[へや]です。

synonyms.note: ところで shifts to a new, unrelated topic; ちなみに adds a detail related to the current one.

related.note: そういえば brings up something just recalled; ちなみに offers a deliberate supplementary note.

title: っこない
meaning: there's no chance of ~; definitely won't / can't
summary: っこない attaches to the ます-stem to flatly deny that something could ever happen — 分かりっこない = 'there's no way I'd understand', 勝てっこない = 'we can't possibly win'. It is a casual, spoken way to voice the speaker's firm conviction that something is impossible, close in meaning to はずがない but far more colloquial.
pitfalls: Attach it to the ます-stem, not the dictionary form: 勝てっこない, not 勝つっこない.
It belongs to casual, spoken Japanese; avoid it in formal writing, where はずがない or わけがない fit better.
It states the speaker's own strong belief that something is impossible, not an objective fact.

examples.ja: 宝くじなんて、そう簡単に当たりっこないよ。
examples.en: There's no way you'll win the lottery that easily.
examples.f: ｜宝[たから]くじなんて、そう｜簡単[かんたん]に｜当[あ]たりっこないよ。

examples.ja: いくら急いでも、終電に間に合いっこない。
examples.en: No matter how much I hurry, there's no chance I'll make the last train.
examples.f: いくら｜急[いそ]いでも、｜終電[しゅうでん]に｜間に合[まにあ]いっこない。

synonyms.note: わけがない also denies possibility but is neutral in register; っこない is distinctly casual and spoken.
はずがない reasons that something 'can't be so'; っこない is a blunter, colloquial 'no way it'll happen'.

related.note: まい is a formal/written negative conjecture ('surely won't'); っこない carries the same certainty in casual speech.

title: 〜つつ・〜つつも
meaning: while doing ~; even though ~ (concessive つつも)
summary: つつ attaches to the ます-stem and has two uses. Plain つつ means 'while doing ~', marking two actions the same person does at once (a formal, written equivalent of ながら). つつも adds a concessive twist — 'even though / despite ~' — where the two clauses clash, as in 悪いと知りつつも = 'even though I know it's wrong'. Both belong to a literary, formal register.
pitfalls: Attach it to the ます-stem: 考えつつ, not 考えるつつ.
Both clauses must share the same subject, just like ながら.
つつ is formal and mostly written; in everyday speech ながら is the natural choice.

examples.ja: 資料を確認しつつ、会議の準備を進めた。
examples.en: I moved ahead with preparing for the meeting while checking the materials.
examples.f: ｜資料[しりょう]を｜確認[かくにん]しつつ、｜会議[かいぎ]の｜準備[じゅんび]を｜進[すす]めた。

examples.ja: 体に悪いと知りつつも、つい甘い物を食べてしまう。
examples.en: Even though I know it's bad for my health, I can't help eating sweets.
examples.f: ｜体[からだ]に｜悪[わる]いと｜知[し]りつつも、つい｜甘[あま]い｜物[もの]を｜食[た]べてしまう。

synonyms.note: ながら is the everyday word for doing two things at once; つつ is its formal, written counterpart.
ながらも matches the concessive つつも ('even though'); ながらも is somewhat less literary.

related.note: つつある uses the same つつ but means 'in the process of ~', describing gradual change, not two simultaneous actions.

title: つつある
meaning: to be in the process of ~; to be gradually ~ing
summary: つつある attaches to the ます-stem to say a change is steadily under way and moving toward a certain state — 減りつつある = 'is gradually decreasing', 回復しつつある = 'is on the way to recovering'. It emphasizes a continuous progression in one direction and, like つつ, has a formal, written flavor. It pairs most naturally with verbs of change.
pitfalls: Attach it to the ます-stem: 変わりつつある, not 変わるつつある.
Unlike a plain ている, つつある stresses a gradual, ongoing shift toward a new state, so it suits change verbs (増える, 減る, 治る) rather than momentary actions.
It is formal and largely written; in conversation ている is more usual.

examples.ja: この町の人口は、年々減りつつある。
examples.en: The population of this town is steadily declining year by year.
examples.f: この｜町[まち]の｜人口[じんこう]は、｜年々[ねんねん]｜減[へ]りつつある。

examples.ja: 医療技術の進歩で、その病気は治りつつある。
examples.en: With advances in medical technology, that illness is gradually being cured.
examples.f: ｜医療[いりょう]｜技術[ぎじゅつ]の｜進歩[しんぽ]で、その｜病気[びょうき]は｜治[なお]りつつある。

related.note: Plain つつ means 'while doing ~' (two simultaneous actions); つつある means a single change is ongoing.

title: ていては
meaning: if one keeps doing ~ (a bad result will follow)
summary: ていては takes the ている form and adds は to say that continuing an action will lead to an undesirable outcome — 遊んでいては = 'if you keep playing (you'll fail)'. It frames an ongoing habit or state as the cause of a coming problem, so the second clause is almost always negative. In casual speech ていては often contracts to てちゃ.
pitfalls: The clause that follows is normally a bad consequence (won't make it, can't succeed), not a neutral result.
In casual speech ていては shrinks to てちゃ (飲んでちゃ); the meaning stays the same.
It criticizes a continuing action or state; for a one-off condition, plain たら or ば is more natural.

examples.ja: そんなに毎日お酒を飲んでいては、体を壊しますよ。
examples.en: If you keep drinking every day like that, you'll ruin your health.
examples.f: そんなに｜毎日[まいにち]お｜酒[さけ]を｜飲[の]んでいては、｜体[からだ]を｜壊[こわ]しますよ。

examples.ja: 細かいことばかり気にしていては、前に進めない。
examples.en: If you keep fretting over every little detail, you can't move forward.
examples.f: ｜細[こま]かいことばかり｜気[き]にしていては、｜前[まえ]に｜進[すす]めない。

related.note: ては is the base pattern for 'if ~, then a bad result'; ていては applies it specifically to a continuing action or state.

title: 〜て以来
meaning: ever since ~; since (a past event)
summary: 以来 marks a point in the past after which a situation has continued unchanged up to now. It follows either the て-form of a verb (卒業して以来 = 'ever since graduating') or a noun (入社以来 = 'ever since joining the company'). The event is a single past change, and the clause that follows describes a state that has held ever since.
pitfalls: 以来 marks a one-time past event as a starting point; it does not work for repeated or ongoing actions.
The following clause describes a lasting state or tendency that continues to the present, not a single later event.
For close, recent time frames (yesterday, this morning) 以来 sounds odd; it implies a stretch of time has passed.

examples.ja: 大学を卒業して以来、彼とは一度も会っていない。
examples.en: I haven't seen him even once since I graduated from university.
examples.f: ｜大学[だいがく]を｜卒業[そつぎょう]して｜以来[いらい]、｜彼[かれ]とは｜一[いち]｜度[ど]も｜会[あ]っていない。

examples.ja: この製品は、発売以来ずっと人気が続いている。
examples.en: This product has stayed popular ever since it went on sale.
examples.f: この｜製品[せいひん]は、｜発売[はつばい]｜以来[いらい]ずっと｜人気[にんき]が｜続[つづ]いている。

synonyms.note: てから simply means 'after doing ~'; 以来 adds that the resulting state has lasted continuously up to now.

title: てこそ
meaning: only by doing ~; it is precisely because one does ~
summary: てこそ combines the て-form with the emphatic particle こそ to single out an action as the essential condition for a valued result — 努力してこそ成功する = 'it is only through effort that one succeeds'. The clause after it is normally positive and desirable: the point is that the good outcome is possible only because of the highlighted action.
pitfalls: The following clause is usually a positive or worthwhile result, since てこそ praises the condition that makes it possible.
It presents the action as the one indispensable condition; a plain から just gives a reason without that emphasis.

examples.ja: 困難を乗り越えてこそ、人は成長できる。
examples.en: It is precisely by overcoming hardships that people grow.
examples.f: ｜困難[こんなん]を｜乗り越[のりこ]えてこそ、｜人[ひと]は｜成長[せいちょう]できる。

examples.ja: 努力を続けてこそ、本当の実力が身につく。
examples.en: Only by keeping up the effort does one gain real ability.
examples.f: ｜努力[どりょく]を｜続[つづ]けてこそ、｜本当[ほんとう]の｜実力[じつりょく]が｜身[み]につく。

synonyms.note: て初めて means 'not until ~ did ...', stressing a first realization; てこそ stresses the essential condition for a good result.

related.note: こそ is the underlying emphatic particle ('precisely'); てこそ applies it to a verb as the key condition.
ばこそ ('precisely because') is a more formal, literary way to stress a reason; てこそ focuses on an enabling action.

title: でしかない
meaning: is nothing but ~; is merely ~
summary: でしかない follows a noun to dismiss it as 'nothing more than ~' — 言い訳でしかない = 'is merely an excuse'. Built from で + しか + ない, it belittles the thing named, saying it does not rise above that limited status. It carries a judgmental, often disparaging tone.
pitfalls: It attaches to a noun; it caps the thing's worth at 'no more than that', usually with a dismissive nuance.
The tone is evaluative, not neutral — the speaker is downplaying or belittling the noun.

examples.ja: それはただの言い訳でしかない。
examples.en: That is nothing but an excuse.
examples.f: それはただの｜言い訳[いいわけ]でしかない。

examples.ja: 今の私にとって、お金は道具でしかない。
examples.en: To me right now, money is merely a tool.
examples.f: ｜今[いま]の｜私[わたし]にとって、お｜金[かね]は｜道具[どうぐ]でしかない。

synonyms.note: にすぎない also means 'no more than ~'; でしかない tends to sound more blunt and dismissive.
しか～ない limits options ('only ~'); でしかない specifically downgrades a noun to 'merely that'.

title: てたまらない
meaning: unbearably ~; can't stand how ~; dying to ~
summary: てたまらない expresses a feeling or desire so strong the speaker can hardly bear it — 暑くてたまらない = 'unbearably hot', 会いたくてたまらない = 'dying to see someone'. It attaches to the て-form of adjectives and verbs of emotion or sensation. たまらない literally means 'cannot be endured', so the whole phrase conveys an overwhelming, uncontrollable state.
pitfalls: It describes the speaker's own uncontrollable feeling or sensation, so it pairs with emotion and sensation words, not neutral statements.
For a desire, it attaches to the 〜たい form (見たくてたまらない), not the plain verb.

examples.ja: 久しぶりの故郷が懐かしくてたまらない。
examples.en: I miss my hometown, which I haven't seen in ages, terribly.
examples.f: ｜久[ひさ]しぶりの｜故郷[こきょう]が｜懐[なつ]かしくてたまらない。

examples.ja: 新しいゲームがやりたくてたまらない。
examples.en: I'm dying to play the new game.
examples.f: ｜新[あたら]しいゲームがやりたくてたまらない。

synonyms.note: てならない conveys the same overwhelming feeling but leans formal and favors spontaneous thoughts (思えてならない).
てしょうがない・てしかたがない is the more casual 'can't help feeling'; てたまらない stresses that the feeling is barely bearable.

title: てちょうだい
meaning: please do ~ (soft, casual request)
summary: てちょうだい follows the て-form to make a gentle, casual request — 取ってちょうだい = 'pass it to me, would you'. It is softer and more familiar than てください, and is used mainly among family and close acquaintances, often by women or when speaking to children. It carries a warm, coaxing tone rather than a formal one.
pitfalls: It is casual and familiar; use てください with people you must be polite to.
It sounds gentle and is associated with women's speech and talking to children, so it can feel out of place from a man in a neutral setting.

examples.ja: ごめん、その塩を取ってちょうだい。
examples.en: Sorry, could you pass me that salt?
examples.f: ごめん、その｜塩[しお]を｜取[と]ってちょうだい。

examples.ja: 宿題が終わったら、すぐに教えてちょうだい。
examples.en: Once you finish your homework, let me know right away.
examples.f: ｜宿題[しゅくだい]が｜終[お]わったら、すぐに｜教[おし]えてちょうだい。

synonyms.note: てください is the standard polite request; てちょうだい is softer, casual, and more intimate.

related.note: てほしい states a wish for someone to act ('I want you to ~'); てちょうだい directly makes the request.

title: てでも
meaning: even if one has to ~ (extreme means)
summary: てでも follows the て-form to name an extreme measure one is willing to take to reach a goal — 借金してでも = 'even if I have to borrow money'. It highlights a drastic action offered as the means, and the main clause states a strong wish or determination to achieve the goal despite that cost.
pitfalls: It names the extreme means one will resort to; the main clause expresses firm will or a strong desire.
Don't confuse it with plain ても ('even if'): てでも specifically presents an action as the drastic method used to accomplish something.

examples.ja: 借金をしてでも、この土地を手に入れたい。
examples.en: I want to get this land, even if I have to go into debt for it.
examples.f: ｜借金[しゃっきん]をしてでも、この｜土地[とち]を｜手[て]に｜入[い]れたい。

examples.ja: 徹夜してでも、明日までにこの仕事を終わらせる。
examples.en: I'll finish this work by tomorrow even if I have to stay up all night.
examples.f: ｜徹夜[てつや]してでも、｜明日[あした]までにこの｜仕事[しごと]を｜終[お]わらせる。

synonyms.note: てまで also marks going to extremes, but often to criticize the excess; てでも stresses one's willingness and resolve.

related.note: ても is plain 'even if ~'; てでも adds でも to frame an extreme action as the means to an end.

title: て当然だ
meaning: it's only natural that ~; no wonder ~
summary: て当然だ follows the て-form to say that a result is entirely natural or deserved given the circumstances — 怒られて当然だ = 'no wonder you got scolded / you deserved it'. It presents an outcome as the obvious, reasonable consequence of what came before, and can carry a 'that's what you get' nuance. It also appears as 〜のも当然だ.
pitfalls: It judges a result as natural and deserved, so it often carries a 'serves you right' or 'of course' tone.
It comments on why an outcome makes sense; it does not predict that something should happen the way はずだ does.

examples.ja: あんな失礼な態度を取れば、怒られて当然だ。
examples.en: If you act that rudely, it's only natural to get scolded.
examples.f: あんな｜失礼[しつれい]な｜態度[たいど]を｜取[と]れば、｜怒[おこ]られて｜当然[とうぜん]だ。

examples.ja: 毎日練習しているのだから、上手になって当然だ。
examples.en: Since he practices every day, no wonder he's gotten good.
examples.f: ｜毎日[まいにち]｜練習[れんしゅう]しているのだから、｜上手[じょうず]になって｜当然[とうぜん]だ。

related.note: はずだ predicts what should logically be the case; て当然だ judges an actual result as natural and deserved.

title: てならない
meaning: can't help feeling ~; ~ terribly
summary: てならない follows the て-form to say a feeling or impression wells up beyond the speaker's control — 気になってならない = 'I can't help worrying', 思えてならない = 'I can't help feeling that ...'. It often attaches to verbs of spontaneous thought and emotion. Similar to てたまらない, it leans somewhat formal and is especially common with 気がする, 思える, and the like.
pitfalls: It works best with spontaneous feelings and impressions (思えてならない, 気になってならない), not deliberate actions.
It is a touch more formal and written than てたまらない, which sounds more everyday.

examples.ja: 試験の結果が気になってならない。
examples.en: I can't help worrying about the exam results.
examples.f: ｜試験[しけん]の｜結果[けっか]が｜気[き]になってならない。

examples.ja: 彼の話は何かおかしいと思えてならない。
examples.en: I can't help feeling there's something off about his story.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]の｜話[はなし]は｜何[なに]かおかしいと｜思[おも]えてならない。

synonyms.note: てたまらない stresses a feeling almost too strong to bear; てならない stresses a feeling that arises on its own and won't stop.
てしょうがない is the more casual 'can't help ~'; てならない is somewhat more formal and literary.

title: ては
meaning: if ~ (a bad result follows); whenever ~
summary: ては joins the て-form with は to set up a condition whose consequence is usually undesirable — 急いでは失敗する = 'if you rush, you'll fail'. It presents the action as a recurring or ongoing cause and leads into a negative outcome. In casual speech it contracts to ちゃ (or じゃ after voiced sounds).
pitfalls: The result clause is normally negative — a problem, failure, or something the speaker wants to avoid.
In casual speech ては becomes ちゃ and では becomes じゃ (やっては → やっちゃ).
This conditional ては differs from the everyday たら/と: it specifically frames the condition as leading to a bad result.

examples.ja: こんなに毎日残業しては、体がもたない。
examples.en: If I keep working overtime every day like this, my body won't hold up.
examples.f: こんなに｜毎日[まいにち]｜残業[ざんぎょう]しては、｜体[からだ]がもたない。

examples.ja: そんなに慌てては、かえって失敗するよ。
examples.en: If you rush like that, you'll only end up making mistakes.
examples.f: そんなに｜慌[あわ]てては、かえって｜失敗[しっぱい]するよ。

synonyms.note: たら is a neutral 'if / when ~'; ては specifically frames the condition as leading to an unwanted result.
と states a natural or automatic consequence; ては highlights the condition as the cause of something bad.

related.note: ていては is the ている version, stressing that a continuing action or state brings the bad result.

title: ては〜ては
meaning: doing ~ and ~ over and over (repeated alternating actions)
summary: Pairing two て-form verbs with は describes a set of actions repeated in alternation — 書いては消し、書いては消し = 'writing and erasing, over and over'. The two verbs are usually opposite or complementary, and the pattern paints a vivid picture of the same cycle happening again and again.
pitfalls: The two verbs typically form a contrasting or paired cycle (write/erase, come/go), not two unrelated actions.
It emphasizes repetition; the sentence usually continues into a description of the ongoing scene or its effect.

examples.ja: 彼女は日記を書いては消し、書いては消して、なかなか進まなかった。
examples.en: She wrote and erased, wrote and erased in her diary, making little progress.
examples.f: ｜彼女[かのじょ]は｜日記[にっき]を｜書[か]いては｜消[け]し、｜書[か]いては｜消[け]して、なかなか｜進[すす]まなかった。

examples.ja: 波が寄せては返し、寄せては返す。
examples.en: The waves surge in and roll back, surge in and roll back.
examples.f: ｜波[なみ]が｜寄[よ]せては｜返[かえ]し、｜寄[よ]せては｜返[かえ]す。

related.note: Single ては sets up a condition with a bad result; the doubled ては〜ては paints repeated, alternating actions.

title: てはいられない
meaning: can't afford to stay ~; can't just keep ~ing
summary: てはいられない is the negative potential of ている plus は — 'cannot remain in this state'. It says the speaker cannot afford to keep doing something or stay as they are because circumstances demand action — のんびりしてはいられない = 'I can't afford to take it easy'. It conveys urgency or emotional pressure to stop and act.
pitfalls: It means one cannot stay in the current action or state because something more pressing calls for action.
The driving force is often urgency or emotion — you feel you must not just sit still.

examples.ja: 締め切りが近いのだから、のんびりしてはいられない。
examples.en: The deadline is near, so I can't afford to take it easy.
examples.f: ｜締め切[しめき]りが｜近[ちか]いのだから、のんびりしてはいられない。

examples.ja: 友達が困っているのを、黙って見てはいられなかった。
examples.en: I couldn't just stand by and watch my friend struggle.
examples.f: ｜友達[ともだち]が｜困[こま]っているのを、｜黙[だま]って｜見[み]てはいられなかった。

synonyms.note: てばかりはいられない adds ばかり ('only'), stressing you can't do just that one thing forever; てはいられない is the plain 'can't stay as I am'.

title: てばかりはいられない
kana: てばかりはいられない
meaning: can't just keep ~ing (something else needs doing)
summary: てばかりはいられない combines て + ばかり ('only') + はいられない to say one cannot go on doing just this one thing — 落ち込んでばかりはいられない = 'I can't just keep moping'. It acknowledges the action but insists it can't continue as the only thing, because other responsibilities call. The tone is one of pulling oneself together to move on.
structure: Verb［て form］＋ばかりはいられない
pitfalls: The ばかり ('only') is key: it says you can't do just this and nothing else, implying you must also do something more constructive.
It usually signals a resolve to stop dwelling and take action, so a positive next step often follows.

examples.ja: 落ち込んでばかりはいられない。前を向いて進もう。
examples.en: I can't just keep moping. Let's face forward and move on.
examples.f: ｜落ち込[おちこ]んでばかりはいられない。｜前[まえ]を｜向[む]いて｜進[すす]もう。

examples.ja: 親に頼ってばかりはいられないので、そろそろ自立したい。
examples.en: I can't keep relying on my parents forever, so I want to become independent soon.
examples.f: ｜親[おや]に｜頼[たよ]ってばかりはいられないので、そろそろ｜自立[じりつ]したい。

synonyms.note: てはいられない simply says you can't stay as you are; てばかりはいられない stresses you can't do only that one thing.

title: てはならない
meaning: must not ~; may not ~ (formal prohibition)
summary: てはならない follows the て-form to state a firm, often official prohibition — してはならない = 'must not do'. It is more formal and weighty than てはいけない, and is common in rules, laws, morals, and written instructions where a norm applies to everyone rather than to one person in the moment.
pitfalls: It is formal and impersonal, fitting rules, laws, and moral principles more than casual one-to-one prohibitions.
Everyday spoken prohibitions usually take てはいけない or だめ; てはならない sounds official or literary.

examples.ja: 試験中は、絶対にカンニングをしてはならない。
examples.en: During the exam, you must never cheat.
examples.f: ｜試験[しけん]｜中[ちゅう]は、｜絶対[ぜったい]にカンニングをしてはならない。

examples.ja: この秘密を、誰にも話してはならない。
examples.en: You must not tell this secret to anyone.
examples.f: この｜秘密[ひみつ]を、｜誰[だれ]にも｜話[はな]してはならない。

synonyms.note: てはいけない is the everyday 'must not'; てはならない is more formal and used for rules and moral norms.

antonyms.note: なければならない is the positive obligation 'must do'; てはならない is the prohibition 'must not do'.

title: 手前
meaning: seeing as ~; given one's position before others
summary: 手前 as a grammar pattern means 'because of one's standing or appearance in front of others, one has to ~'. Following a noun + の or a plain-form verb, it gives a reason rooted in pride, face, or obligation toward the people watching — 約束した手前 = 'having promised (and with others aware), I can't back out'. The following clause states what one must or cannot do to save face.
pitfalls: This 手前 gives a reason based on one's face or position before others; it is not the literal 手前 meaning 'in front of / this side'.
The main clause states an obligation or restraint one accepts to keep up appearances (can't refuse, can't complain).

examples.ja: 後輩たちの手前、弱音を吐くわけにはいかない。
examples.en: With my juniors watching, I can't let myself complain.
examples.f: ｜後輩[こうはい]たちの｜手前[てまえ]、｜弱音[よわね]を｜吐[は]くわけにはいかない。

examples.ja: 一度引き受けると言った手前、今さら断れない。
examples.en: Having said I'd take it on, I can't very well refuse now.
examples.f: ｜一度[いちど]｜引き受[ひきう]けると｜言[い]った｜手前[てまえ]、｜今[いま]さら｜断[ことわ]れない。

synonyms.note: 以上は gives a logical 'now that ~, naturally ~'; 手前 grounds the obligation specifically in appearances before others.
からには means 'now that / so long as ~', stressing resolve; 手前 stresses saving face in front of people.

related.note: 上は means 'now that ~ (I've done it), I must ~'; 手前 adds the specific motive of pride or appearances.

title: てまで
meaning: going so far as to ~; to the extreme of ~
summary: てまで follows the て-form to describe going to an extreme length to achieve something — 借金してまで = 'going so far as to borrow money'. It is frequently used to question or criticize whether such an extreme is worth it, as in 〜てまでする必要はない = 'there's no need to go that far'. The nuance often leans skeptical or disapproving.
pitfalls: It often carries a critical or doubtful tone — the speaker questions whether going to that extreme is justified.
Compare てでも, which frames the same extreme as one's own firm resolve; てまで more often evaluates the extreme from the outside.

examples.ja: 健康を害してまで、働き続ける必要はない。
examples.en: There's no need to keep working to the point of wrecking your health.
examples.f: ｜健康[けんこう]を｜害[がい]してまで、｜働[はたら]き｜続[つづ]ける｜必要[ひつよう]はない。

examples.ja: 行列に何時間も並んでまで、その店で食べたいとは思わない。
examples.en: I don't want to eat at that shop badly enough to stand in line for hours.
examples.f: ｜行列[ぎょうれつ]に｜何[なん]｜時間[じかん]も｜並[なら]んでまで、その｜店[みせ]で｜食[た]べたいとは｜思[おも]わない。

synonyms.note: てでも frames an extreme means as one's own determination; てまで often questions or criticizes the extreme.

title: ということは
meaning: which means; that is to say; so that means
summary: ということは takes a known fact or statement and draws the logical conclusion that follows from it — 'which means / so that means'. 電気がついているということは = 'the lights are on, which means...'. It often stands at the head of a sentence as a connector (ということは、〜) to walk the listener through an inference.
structure: Sentence［plain form］＋ ということは
pitfalls: Distinguish from ということだ, which reports hearsay or restates a definition; ということは draws your own inference from something already known.
The concluding clause usually states a deduction (〜のだろう・はずだ・わけだ), since ということは introduces the reasoning that leads to it.

examples.ja: 電気がついているということは、彼はもう帰っているはずだ。
examples.en: The lights are on, which means he must already be home.
examples.f: ｜電気[でんき]がついているということは、｜彼[かれ]はもう｜帰[かえ]っているはずだ。

examples.ja: 明日は祝日か。ということは、銀行は閉まっているね。
examples.en: Tomorrow's a holiday, huh. Which means the banks will be closed.
examples.f: ｜明日[あした]は｜祝日[しゅくじつ]か。ということは、｜銀行[ぎんこう]は｜閉[し]まっているね。

synonyms.note: つまり restates the same content more simply ('in other words'); ということは derives a fresh consequence from it.

related.note: ということだ reports what was heard or defines a term; ということは reasons out what a fact implies.
というわけだ presents the resulting explanation ('that's why'); ということは explicitly walks through the inference to reach it.

title: という点から考えると
kana: というてんからかんがえると
romaji: to iu ten kara kangaeru to
meaning: considering it from the standpoint of; in terms of the point that
summary: という点から考えると frames a judgment from one particular angle or criterion — 'considering it from the standpoint of ~ / when you think about it in terms of ~'. It is formal, essay-style Japanese that names the perspective from which an evaluation is made before delivering it.
structure: Noun ＋ という点から考えると
Sentence［plain form］＋ という点から考えると
pitfalls: This is written, formal register; in casual speech から見ると ('from the viewpoint of') sounds more natural.
The 点 names the specific aspect being weighed, so it pairs with a following judgment about that aspect.

examples.ja: 安全という点から考えると、この設計にはまだ問題がある。
examples.en: Considering it from the standpoint of safety, this design still has problems.
examples.f: ｜安全[あんぜん]という｜点[てん]から｜考[かんが]えると、この｜設計[せっけい]にはまだ｜問題[もんだい]がある。

examples.ja: 費用がかかるという点から考えると、この計画は現実的ではない。
examples.en: In terms of the point that it is costly, this plan is not realistic.
examples.f: ｜費用[ひよう]がかかるという｜点[てん]から｜考[かんが]えると、この｜計画[けいかく]は｜現実[げんじつ]｜的[てき]ではない。

synonyms.note: から見ると is the concise, general 'from the viewpoint of'; という点から考えると explicitly names a stated criterion (点) and is more formal.

related.note: にとって marks whose perspective something matters to ('for ~'); という点から考えると names the criterion used to evaluate it.

title: というふうに
meaning: in a way like; in such a manner (that)
summary: というふうに describes the manner or way something is done or said — 'in a way like ~ / in such a manner'. It often follows a quoted content or a concrete example to characterize how an action proceeds: まず洗って、次に切る、というふうに… The related こういうふうに／そういうふうに mean 'like this / like that'.
pitfalls: というふうに characterizes the manner of an action; it is more colloquial than the ように of manner but works the same way.
It typically leads into a verb describing how something is done, not into a following noun.

examples.ja: 子供たちに、まず手を洗い、次にうがいをする、というふうに順番を教えた。
examples.en: I taught the children the order in a way like: first wash your hands, then gargle.
examples.f: ｜子供[こども]たちに、まず｜手[て]を｜洗[あら]い、｜次[つぎ]にうがいをする、というふうに｜順番[じゅんばん]を｜教[おし]えた。

examples.ja: 使った物は元の場所に戻す、というふうに習慣づけている。
examples.en: I've trained myself into the habit, in the manner of always putting used things back where they were.
examples.f: ｜使[つか]った｜物[もの]は｜元[もと]の｜場所[ばしょ]に｜戻[もど]す、というふうに｜習慣[しゅうかん]づけている。

synonyms.note: ように also expresses 'in the manner that'; というふうに is more conversational and often follows a quoted example.

title: というものだ
meaning: that really is ~; that's what you call ~ (emphatic assertion)
summary: というものだ makes an emphatic, often evaluative assertion about the true nature of something — 'that really is ~ / that's what you call ~'. 助け合うのが友情というものだ = 'helping each other is what friendship truly is'. The speaker states a general truth or firm judgment, frequently with a reflective or critical tone.
structure: Sentence［plain form］＋ というものだ
pitfalls: Don't confuse it with the negative というものではない ('it's not necessarily so'); というものだ affirms strongly.
It voices conviction about how something essentially is, not a neutral description of a single event.

examples.ja: 困ったときに助け合うのが、本当の友情というものだ。
examples.en: Helping each other in hard times — that's what true friendship really is.
examples.f: ｜困[こま]ったときに｜助け合[たすけあ]うのが、｜本当[ほんとう]の｜友情[ゆうじょう]というものだ。

examples.ja: 締め切りを守らないのは、社会人として無責任というものだ。
examples.en: Failing to meet deadlines is, for a working adult, truly irresponsible.
examples.f: ｜締め切[しめき]りを｜守[まも]らないのは、｜社会[しゃかい]｜人[じん]として｜無責任[むせきにん]というものだ。

synonyms.note: ものだ states general truths or 'should' advice; というものだ frames a stronger, evaluative assertion about a thing's essential nature.

antonyms.note: というものではない is the direct counter — 'it's not necessarily the case that ~'.

title: というものではない・というものでもない
kana: というものではない・というものでもない
romaji: to iu mono dewa nai / to iu mono demo nai
meaning: it's not necessarily the case that; it's not as simple as
summary: というものではない denies that something is absolutely or universally true — 'it's not necessarily the case that ~ / it's not as simple as ~'. It pushes back on an over-generalized assumption, often that doing X automatically brings a good result: お金があれば幸せというものではない. The でもない variant is a slightly softer 'nor is it that'.
structure: Sentence［plain form］＋ というものではない
Sentence［plain form］＋ というものでもない
pitfalls: It rejects an over-generalization, not the claim entirely; it says 'not always', not 'never'.
Contrast というわけではない, which corrects a specific inferred conclusion; というものではない targets a sweeping 'if X then always Y' assumption.

examples.ja: お金があれば幸せになれるというものではない。
examples.en: Having money doesn't necessarily mean you can be happy.
examples.f: お｜金[かね]があれば｜幸[しあわ]せになれるというものではない。

examples.ja: 謝れば済むというものでもない。
examples.en: It's not as if simply apologizing settles everything.
examples.f: ｜謝[あやま]れば｜済[す]むというものでもない。

synonyms.note: とは限らない also means 'not necessarily so'; というものではない specifically rejects an 'if X, then always Y' generalization.
必ずしも is the adverb 'not always' that pairs with a negative; というものではない is the full clause-ending pattern expressing it.

antonyms.note: というものだ asserts strongly that something truly is a certain way; というものではない denies it holds absolutely.

related.note: というわけではない softly denies a specific inferred conclusion; というものではない denies a general rule.

title: というわけではない
meaning: it's not that ~; it doesn't mean that ~ (partial denial)
summary: というわけではない softly denies a conclusion the listener might draw — 'it's not that ~ / it doesn't mean that ~'. 嫌いというわけではない = 'it's not that I dislike it (I just...)'. It corrects a likely misunderstanding without denying everything, so it is a hedged, partial negation.
structure: Sentence［plain form］＋ というわけではない
pitfalls: It negates a specific inferred conclusion, not the whole situation; something else is usually true instead.
Compare というものではない, which denies an over-generalized rule; わけ targets the particular conclusion someone might jump to.

examples.ja: 毎日料理をするが、料理が好きというわけではない。
examples.en: I cook every day, but it's not that I actually like cooking.
examples.f: ｜毎日[まいにち]｜料理[りょうり]をするが、｜料理[りょうり]が｜好[す]きというわけではない。

examples.ja: 全部読んだが、内容を理解したというわけではない。
examples.en: I read all of it, but that doesn't mean I understood the content.
examples.f: ｜全部[ぜんぶ]｜読[よ]んだが、｜内容[ないよう]を｜理解[りかい]したというわけではない。

synonyms.note: わけではない is the same partial denial without という; adding という foregrounds a stated or implied claim being corrected.

related.note: からといって ('just because ~') often sets up the assumption that というわけではない then denies.
というものではない denies a general 'X always leads to Y' rule; というわけではない denies one specific conclusion.

title: といった
meaning: (things) such as A and B; like
summary: といった follows two or more representative items and leads into the category they belong to — '(things) such as A and B'. サッカーやテニスといったスポーツ = 'sports such as soccer and tennis'. It presents the listed items as examples of a broader group named right after.
pitfalls: といった is followed by a summarizing noun (the category); here it is not the past tense of と言う.
Unlike など, which can close a list on its own, といった normally requires the category noun that follows it.

examples.ja: 京都や奈良といった古い町には、外国人観光客が多い。
examples.en: Old cities such as Kyoto and Nara have many foreign tourists.
examples.f: ｜京都[きょうと]や｜奈良[なら]といった｜古[ふる]い｜町[まち]には、｜外国[がいこく]｜人[じん]｜観光[かんこう]｜客[きゃく]が｜多[おお]い。

examples.ja: 頭痛や発熱といった症状が出たら、すぐ病院へ行ってください。
examples.en: If symptoms such as headache and fever appear, go to the hospital right away.
examples.f: ｜頭痛[ずつう]や｜発熱[はつねつ]といった｜症状[しょうじょう]が｜出[で]たら、すぐ｜病院[びょういん]へ｜行[い]ってください。

synonyms.note: など also lists representative examples ('such as / etc.') but can end a list without a following category noun; といった needs one.

title: どうせ
meaning: anyway; after all; no matter what
summary: どうせ is an adverb expressing resigned certainty that an outcome is inevitable — 'anyway / after all / no matter what'. It carries a pessimistic or self-deprecating coloring (どうせ私なんか = 'someone like me, after all'), but can also mean 'since it's going to happen anyway, might as well go all in'.
pitfalls: どうせ adds emotional resignation or inevitability, unlike the neutral とにかく ('anyway, in any case').
It often pairs with んだから／から, leading either into giving up or into a 'might as well do it properly' decision.

examples.ja: どうせ間に合わないんだから、急いでも仕方がない。
examples.en: We won't make it anyway, so there's no point rushing.
examples.f: どうせ｜間に合[まにあ]わないんだから、｜急[いそ]いでも｜仕方[しかた]がない。

examples.ja: どうせやるなら、最後まできちんとやろう。
examples.en: If I'm going to do it anyway, I'll see it through to the end properly.
examples.f: どうせやるなら、｜最後[さいご]まできちんとやろう。

title: どうやら
meaning: apparently; it seems that
summary: どうやら is an adverb that flags a tentative inference from available signs — 'apparently / it seems'. It typically pairs with a conjectural ending like らしい, ようだ, or みたいだ (どうやら風邪をひいたようだ). It softens a guess the speaker is fairly, but not fully, sure of.
structure: どうやら ＋ Sentence（〜らしい／ようだ／みたいだ）
pitfalls: どうやら sets up a guess, so the sentence usually ends in a conjectural form (ようだ・らしい・みたいだ), not a flat assertion.
It signals a fairly confident but still tentative inference, softer than a definite だ.

examples.ja: どうやら彼はこの計画に反対らしい。
examples.en: Apparently he's against this plan.
examples.f: どうやら｜彼[かれ]はこの｜計画[けいかく]に｜反対[はんたい]らしい。

examples.ja: この様子だと、どうやら約束の時間に間に合いそうだ。
examples.en: The way things look, it seems we'll manage to make the appointment on time.
examples.f: この｜様子[ようす]だと、どうやら｜約束[やくそく]の｜時間[じかん]に｜間に合[まにあ]いそうだ。

related.note: らしい is the conjecture ending どうやら commonly leads into; どうやら is the adverb that flags the inference.
ようだ likewise expresses an evidence-based guess; どうやら pairs with it to underline that the conclusion is tentative.

title: とか(で)
meaning: (I heard) something like ~; and reportedly because ~
summary: とか, and especially とかで, reports something heard in a vague, non-committal way — '(I heard) something like ~'. とかで adds a reported reason: 熱があるとかで休んだ = 'he was off, apparently because he had a fever or something'. The speaker signals the information is secondhand and imprecise.
pitfalls: This hearsay/vague とか differs from the listing とか (AとかB, 'things like A and B').
The で adds 'and for that (reported) reason', linking the vague hearsay to a result.

examples.ja: 田中さんは急用ができたとかで、今日は来ないそうだ。
examples.en: Tanaka apparently had something urgent come up, so it seems he won't be here today.
examples.f: ｜田中[たなか]さんは｜急用[きゅうよう]ができたとかで、｜今日[きょう]は｜来[こ]ないそうだ。

examples.ja: 隣の店は改装するとかで、しばらく閉まるらしい。
examples.en: The shop next door is closing for a while — renovating or something, apparently.
examples.f: ｜隣[となり]の｜店[みせ]は｜改装[かいそう]するとかで、しばらく｜閉[し]まるらしい。

synonyms.note: そうだ reports hearsay as heard; とかで is vaguer ('something like') and adds a reported reason with で.

related.note: ということだ reports information as a clear conclusion or definition; とかで keeps it deliberately vague and secondhand.
らしい draws a conjecture from what one has heard; とかで simply relays the vague report as a reason.

title: と考えられる
meaning: it is thought that; it can be considered that
summary: と考えられる is the passive of 考える, used to present a conclusion as an objective, reasoned inference rather than a personal opinion — 'it is thought / it can be considered that'. It is standard in academic and formal writing, where the passive deliberately avoids naming who holds the view.
structure: Sentence［plain form］＋ と考えられる
pitfalls: It states a reasoned, impersonal conclusion; it is more objective and formal than と思う ('I think').
The passive form intentionally leaves the thinker unnamed, presenting the view as generally accepted.

examples.ja: 調査の結果から、原因は気温の変化にあると考えられる。
examples.en: From the results of the survey, the cause is thought to lie in the change in temperature.
examples.f: ｜調査[ちょうさ]の｜結果[けっか]から、｜原因[げんいん]は｜気温[きおん]の｜変化[へんか]にあると｜考[かんが]えられる。

examples.ja: この習慣は江戸時代に始まったと考えられている。
examples.en: This custom is thought to have begun in the Edo period.
examples.f: この｜習慣[しゅうかん]は｜江戸[えど]｜時代[じだい]に｜始[はじ]まったと｜考[かんが]えられている。

synonyms.note: とされる presents something as an established or officially accepted view; と考えられる frames it as a reasoned inference.

related.note: と思う voices a personal opinion; と考えられる states an objective, impersonal conclusion via the passive.

title: どころではない
meaning: this is no time for ~; ~ is out of the question
summary: どころではない says the circumstances make something out of the question — 'this is no time for ~ / I'm in no position to ~'. 忙しくて旅行どころではない = 'I'm too busy — a trip is out of the question'. It strongly rejects an activity as impossible given more pressing conditions.
structure: Verb［dictionary form］＋ どころではない
pitfalls: Don't confuse it with どころか ('far from ~; on the contrary'), which contrasts an expectation with a stronger reality; どころではない rules an activity out due to circumstances.
The rejected activity is usually something minor compared with the pressing situation that overrides it.

examples.ja: 仕事が山ほどあって、昼ご飯を食べるどころではない。
examples.en: I have a mountain of work — eating lunch is out of the question.
examples.f: ｜仕事[しごと]が｜山[やま]ほどあって、｜昼[ひる]ご｜飯[はん]を｜食[た]べるどころではない。

examples.ja: 大きな地震の直後で、旅行どころではなかった。
examples.en: Right after the big earthquake, a trip was out of the question.
examples.f: ｜大[おお]きな｜地震[じしん]の｜直後[ちょくご]で、｜旅行[りょこう]どころではなかった。

related.note: どころか contrasts expectation with a stronger reality ('far from ~'); どころではない says circumstances make something impossible.

title: ところに・ところへ
meaning: just as ~; right when ~ (an event breaks in)
summary: ところに / ところへ marks the precise moment one situation is unfolding when another event breaks in — 'just as ~ / right when ~'. 出かけようとしたところに電話が来た = 'just as I was about to leave, the phone rang'. The second event typically interrupts or coincides with the first.
structure: Verb［dictionary／ている／た form］＋ ところに／ところへ
い-adjective ＋ ところに／ところへ
pitfalls: It needs an intruding event or arrival, often with に／へ marking the point it comes in; this is not the plain 場所 'place'.
に and へ are largely interchangeable here.

examples.ja: 出かけようとしたところに、友達が訪ねてきた。
examples.en: Just as I was about to head out, a friend came to visit.
examples.f: ｜出[で]かけようとしたところに、｜友達[ともだち]が｜訪[たず]ねてきた。

examples.ja: 困っているところへ、先輩が助けに来てくれた。
examples.en: Right when I was struggling, my senior came to help me.
examples.f: ｜困[こま]っているところへ、｜先輩[せんぱい]が｜助[たす]けに｜来[き]てくれた。

related.note: たところ marks the point an action has just finished; ところに／ところへ marks a moment interrupted by another event.

title: ところを見ると
meaning: judging from the fact that ~
summary: ところを見ると draws an inference from an observed fact — 'judging from the fact that ~'. 笑っているところを見ると、うまくいったのだろう = 'judging from the fact that she's smiling, it must have gone well'. The speaker reasons from visible evidence to a likely conclusion, usually ending in a conjecture.
structure: Sentence［plain form］＋ ところを見ると
pitfalls: The clause usually ends in a guess (〜のだろう・らしい・にちがいない), since ところを見ると supplies evidence for an inference rather than a fact.
The evidence is something actually observed, not merely assumed.

examples.ja: あの二人がよく話しているところを見ると、仲がいいのだろう。
examples.en: Judging from how those two often talk, they must get along well.
examples.f: あの｜二[に]｜人[にん]がよく｜話[はな]しているところを｜見[み]ると、｜仲[なか]がいいのだろう。

examples.ja: 電気が消えているところを見ると、彼はもう寝たらしい。
examples.en: Judging from the fact that the lights are off, it seems he's already gone to bed.
examples.f: ｜電気[でんき]が｜消[き]えているところを｜見[み]ると、｜彼[かれ]はもう｜寝[ね]たらしい。

synonyms.note: から見ると can mean 'judging from' too, but also 'from the viewpoint of'; ところを見ると specifically reasons from an observed fact.

related.note: からして also reasons 'judging from' a single telling detail; ところを見ると points to an observed scene as the evidence.

title: として〜ない
meaning: not even a single one; none at all
summary: With a 'one + counter' phrase, 〜として〜ない expresses total negation — 'not even a single one'. 一人として反対しなかった = 'not a single person objected'. The として emphasizes that the negation covers every last member without exception.
structure: 一 ＋ counter ＋ として ＋ … ＋ ない
pitfalls: This として needs a 'one + counter' phrase before it and a negative predicate after; it is not the として meaning 'as / in the role of'.
The result is emphatic 'none at all', stronger than a plain negative.

examples.ja: これまで一度として、彼が約束を破ったことはない。
examples.en: Not even once has he ever broken a promise.
examples.f: これまで｜一[いち]｜度[ど]として、｜彼[かれ]が｜約束[やくそく]を｜破[やぶ]ったことはない。

examples.ja: 彼の話には、一つとして納得できる点がなかった。
examples.en: There was not a single convincing point in his story.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]の｜話[はなし]には、｜一[ひと]つとして｜納得[なっとく]できる｜点[てん]がなかった。

related.note: として on its own means 'as / in the role of'; in 〜として〜ない it instead intensifies a total negation after a 'one + counter' phrase.

title: としては
meaning: as (a) ~; for a ~; speaking as ~
summary: としては sets a standpoint or standard for judgment — 'as (a) ~ / for a ~ / speaking as ~'. 新人としてはよくやっている = 'for a newcomer, she's doing well'; 私としては反対だ = 'as for me, I'm against it'. It frames a judgment against the norm for that role or from that person's position.
pitfalls: Compare にしては ('for ~, contrary to expectation'), which stresses a mismatch with the standard; としては just states the standard or standpoint without implying surprise.
With a person it often means 'speaking for ~ / from ~'s position', not a comparison.

examples.ja: 初めての作品としては、よくできていると思う。
examples.en: For a first work, I think it's very well made.
examples.f: ｜初[はじ]めての｜作品[さくひん]としては、よくできていると｜思[おも]う。

examples.ja: 私としては、その案に賛成しかねます。
examples.en: Speaking for myself, I'm reluctant to support that proposal.
examples.f: ｜私[わたし]としては、その｜案[あん]に｜賛成[さんせい]しかねます。

synonyms.note: として states a role or capacity plainly; としては adds は to foreground that role as the standard or standpoint for what follows.

related.note: にしては means 'for ~' with a note of surprise at not matching the norm; としては states the norm or standpoint without that mismatch.
にとって marks whose interest something concerns ('for ~'); としては sets a standard or position from which a judgment is made.

title: としても
meaning: even if; even assuming that ~
summary: としても supposes a case and concedes that it does not change the outcome — 'even if / even assuming that ~'. 本当だとしても驚かない = 'even if it's true, I won't be surprised'. It combines a hypothetical (とする) with the concessive も.
pitfalls: としても supposes something hypothetically ('even if we assume'), whereas ても can also concede an actual fact; としても leans clearly on a supposition.
After a noun or な-adjective, insert だ: 本当だとしても, not 本当としても.

examples.ja: 今から急いだとしても、始発には間に合わないだろう。
examples.en: Even if we hurry now, we probably won't make the first train.
examples.f: ｜今[いま]から｜急[いそ]いだとしても、｜始発[しはつ]には｜間に合[まにあ]わないだろう。

examples.ja: たとえ冗談だとしても、そんなことは言うべきではない。
examples.en: Even if it's a joke, you shouldn't say such a thing.
examples.f: たとえ｜冗談[じょうだん]だとしても、そんなことは｜言[い]うべきではない。

synonyms.note: ても concedes 'even if / even though', including actual facts; としても adds the sense of supposing a hypothetical case.

related.note: とすれば・としたら supposes a case and reasons forward from it; としても supposes a case but concedes it changes nothing.
たって is the casual spoken 'even if'; としても is the more composed 'even assuming that ~'.

title: とっくに
meaning: long ago; already (a long time back)
summary: とっくに is a casual adverb meaning something happened well before now — 'long ago / already (ages ago)'. とっくに終わったよ = 'it finished ages ago'. It stresses that the event lies far in the past relative to the moment being discussed, often with mild surprise the listener didn't already know.
pitfalls: It emphasizes 'already, a long time ago' and is colloquial, so it goes with a completed or past state.
It is stronger and more casual than a plain すでに ('already').

examples.ja: その本ならとっくに読み終わったよ。
examples.en: That book? I finished it ages ago.
examples.f: その｜本[ほん]ならとっくに｜読[よ]み｜終[お]わったよ。

examples.ja: 彼女はとっくに家を出て、駅に向かっているはずだ。
examples.en: She left home long ago and should be heading to the station by now.
examples.f: ｜彼女[かのじょ]はとっくに｜家[いえ]を｜出[で]て、｜駅[えき]に｜向[む]かっているはずだ。

synonyms.note: すでに is the neutral, more formal 'already'; とっくに is casual and stresses that it was a long time ago.

related.note: もう marks 'already' at or by now; とっくに pushes the timing well back into the past.

title: とも
meaning: even if; no matter (how) ~ (formal concession)
summary: In formal, literary Japanese 〜とも expresses concession — 'even if / no matter (how) ~'. It attaches to a verb's volitional form (何が起ころうとも = 'no matter what happens') or an い-adjective's 〜く form (いかに苦しくとも). The outcome holds regardless of the condition.
pitfalls: This concessive とも is formal and written; ordinary speech uses ても／たとえ〜ても instead.
Don't confuse it with sentence-final とも ('of course') or with 少なくとも／遅くとも ('at the least / at the latest').

examples.ja: どんな困難があろうとも、最後まで諦めないつもりだ。
examples.en: No matter what difficulties there may be, I intend not to give up until the end.
examples.f: どんな｜困難[こんなん]があろうとも、｜最後[さいご]まで｜諦[あきら]めないつもりだ。

examples.ja: いかに時間がかかろうとも、この研究をやり遂げたい。
examples.en: However long it may take, I want to see this research through.
examples.f: いかに｜時間[じかん]がかかろうとも、この｜研究[けんきゅう]をやり｜遂[と]げたい。

synonyms.note: ても is the everyday 'even if / even though'; とも is its formal, literary equivalent, attached to the volitional or 〜く form.

related.note: たって is the casual spoken 'even if'; とも sits at the opposite, most formal end of the register scale.

title: ないことには〜ない
meaning: unless ~ (happens), it won't / can't ~
summary: 〜ないことには〜ない presents the first clause as an indispensable condition: unless that thing is done or comes about, the desirable result in the second clause is impossible. The main clause is always negative — nothing can move forward until the precondition is met. Common with 'try it and see' situations: 使ってみないことには = 'unless you actually try it'.
structure: Verb［ない form］＋ことには ～ない
pitfalls: The main clause must be negative or state an impossibility (～ない, ～できない); a positive result contradicts the pattern.
It frames the first clause as a necessary precondition, not just a cause; nothing can begin until it is satisfied.

examples.ja: 実際に使ってみないことには、この製品の良さは分からない。
examples.en: Unless you actually try it out, you can't appreciate how good this product is.
examples.f: ｜実際[じっさい]に｜使[つか]ってみないことには、この｜製品[せいひん]の｜良[よ]さは｜分[わ]からない。

examples.ja: 予算が承認されないことには、計画を進めることはできません。
examples.en: Unless the budget is approved, we cannot move ahead with the plan.
examples.f: ｜予算[よさん]が｜承認[しょうにん]されないことには、｜計画[けいかく]を｜進[すす]めることはできません。

synonyms.note: てからでないと stresses sequence ('not until after ~'); ないことには frames the clause as a required condition for anything to happen.
ないと is the everyday 'unless / have to'; ないことには is more emphatic that nothing at all can start otherwise.

related.note: なければならない states a plain obligation to do something; ないことには says the result is unreachable without it.

title: ないではいられない
meaning: can't help but ~; can't keep oneself from ~
summary: 〜ないではいられない describes an urge or emotion so strong that you cannot stop yourself from acting on it — 泣かないではいられない = 'I can't help but cry'. The doubled negative (can't-not-do) conveys that the action is spontaneous and beyond the speaker's control, usually driven by feeling. It is most natural in the first person or when describing someone's nature.
structure: Verb［ない form］＋ではいられない
pitfalls: The impulse is involuntary and feeling-driven, not a reasoned decision; it describes what you can't hold back.
Attach it to the ない-form: 言わないではいられない, not 言わなくてはいられない.

examples.ja: あんなに悲しい映画を見ては、泣かないではいられなかった。
examples.en: Watching such a sad movie, I couldn't help but cry.
examples.f: あんなに｜悲[かな]しい｜映画[えいが]を｜見[み]ては、｜泣[な]かないではいられなかった。

examples.ja: 友人が困っているのを見ると、手を貸さないではいられない。
examples.en: When I see a friend in trouble, I can't keep myself from lending a hand.
examples.f: ｜友人[ゆうじん]が｜困[こま]っているのを｜見[み]ると、｜手[て]を｜貸[か]さないではいられない。

synonyms.note: ずにはいられない means the same thing in a slightly more formal, written register.
てならない says a feeling wells up uncontrollably; ないではいられない says you can't stop yourself from acting on it.

related.note: ざるを得ない is being forced by circumstances with no choice; ないではいられない is an inner emotional urge.

title: ないわけにはいかない
kana: ないわけにはいかない
meaning: can't not do; have no choice but to do
summary: 〜ないわけにはいかない expresses obligation that comes from social or psychological pressure: given the circumstances, not doing the action is simply not an option, so you have to do it. 行かないわけにはいかない = 'I can't very well not go'. The reason is usually a duty, expectation, or relationship rather than physical necessity.
structure: Verb［ない form］＋わけにはいかない
pitfalls: The double negative yields strong obligation ('must do'); the positive わけにはいかない means the opposite — 'cannot (afford to) do'.
The compulsion is social or moral, not physical impossibility; it reflects what circumstances won't let you avoid.

examples.ja: 上司に誘われたのだから、飲み会に行かないわけにはいかない。
examples.en: Since my boss invited me, I really can't not go to the drinking party.
examples.f: ｜上司[じょうし]に｜誘[さそ]われたのだから、｜飲[の]み｜会[かい]に｜行[い]かないわけにはいかない。

examples.ja: 大事な会議なので、体調が悪くても出席しないわけにはいかない。
examples.en: It's an important meeting, so even feeling unwell, I have no choice but to attend.
examples.f: ｜大事[だいじ]な｜会議[かいぎ]なので、｜体調[たいちょう]が｜悪[わる]くても｜出席[しゅっせき]しないわけにはいかない。

synonyms.note: ざるを得ない also means 'have no choice but to'; it is more formal and stresses external force rather than social duty.
なければならない is neutral necessity; ないわけにはいかない adds the sense of being socially or morally unable to refuse.

related.note: Positive わけにはいかない means 'cannot do (for such reasons)'; adding ない flips it to 'cannot not do'.

title: なお
meaning: still; even more; furthermore, in addition
summary: なお has two written-language uses. As an adverb it means 'still / even now' or 'even more' — 今なお = still even now, なお一層 = all the more. As a sentence-initial conjunction it adds supplementary information to what was just said — 'note that; in addition'. Both belong to formal writing and announcements rather than casual speech.
structure: なお（一層） ＋ predicate ［still / even more］
pitfalls: The connective なお opens a new sentence to append a side note; the adverb なお sits before a predicate meaning 'still / even more'.
This なお is unrelated to 直す/直る ('to fix / be fixed'), which happen to share the reading.

examples.ja: この問題は、専門家のあいだでもなお議論が続いている。
examples.en: This issue is still under debate even among experts.
examples.f: この｜問題[もんだい]は、｜専門[せんもん]｜家[か]のあいだでもなお｜議論[ぎろん]が｜続[つづ]いている。

examples.ja: 会議は来週の月曜に始まります。なお、資料は当日お配りします。
examples.en: The meeting starts next Monday. In addition, materials will be handed out on the day.
examples.f: ｜会議[かいぎ]は｜来週[らいしゅう]の｜月曜[げつよう]に｜始[はじ]まります。なお、｜資料[しりょう]は｜当日[とうじつ]お｜配[くば]りします。

synonyms.note: さらに means 'furthermore / even more' and is usable in speech; なお is more formal and typical of written notices.
に加えて adds one thing on top of another as 'in addition to ~'; なお loosely appends a supplementary remark.

title: 中を・中では
meaning: in the midst of; amid (often adverse or busy) conditions
summary: 〜中を・〜中で(は) marks a surrounding situation — often busy, difficult, or inconvenient — against which something is nonetheless done. Here 中 is figurative ('amid such circumstances'), not a literal inside. 中を tends to accompany an action carried out despite the conditions, as in the set polite phrase お忙しい中を ('amid your busy schedule'); 中で(は) frames the prevailing situation.
pitfalls: 中 here is figurative — 'amid a situation' — not a physical interior.
中を commonly appears in fixed polite openings such as お忙しい中を / お寒い中を, thanking someone for acting despite the conditions.

examples.ja: ご多忙の中を、わざわざお越しいただきありがとうございます。
examples.en: Thank you for taking the trouble to come amid your busy schedule.
examples.f: ご｜多忙[たぼう]の｜中[なか]を、わざわざお｜越[こ]しいただきありがとうございます。

examples.ja: 大雨の中で、選手たちは最後まで試合を続けた。
examples.en: In the midst of heavy rain, the players kept playing to the very end.
examples.f: ｜大雨[おおあめ]の｜中[なか]で、｜選手[せんしゅ]たちは｜最後[さいご]まで｜試合[しあい]を｜続[つづ]けた。

related.note: 最中に pinpoints the exact moment an action is underway; 中を・中では frames a broader surrounding condition.
うちに means 'while a state lasts (before it changes)'; 中で(は) simply sets the prevailing circumstances.

title: なくて済む
meaning: get by without doing; end up not having to do
summary: 〜なくて済む describes a situation that works out so that you are spared having to do something — usually a relief. 待たなくて済む = 'I don't have to wait after all'. It reports a fortunate outcome, not a decision or a rule; something about the situation removes the burden. The more formal written equivalent is 〜ずに済む.
structure: Verb［ない form］＋済む （〜なくて済む／〜ないで済む）
pitfalls: It reports an outcome you happen to be spared, not a choice or permission not to do.
Distinguish from なくてもいい, which grants permission ('you don't have to'); なくて済む says circumstances let you off the hook.

examples.ja: 友達が車で送ってくれたので、タクシーを使わなくて済んだ。
examples.en: A friend gave me a ride, so I didn't have to take a taxi after all.
examples.f: ｜友達[ともだち]が｜車[くるま]で｜送[おく]ってくれたので、タクシーを｜使[つか]わなくて｜済[す]んだ。

examples.ja: 予約しておけば、店で長く待たなくて済みます。
examples.en: If you book ahead, you won't have to wait long at the restaurant.
examples.f: ｜予約[よやく]しておけば、｜店[みせ]で｜長[なが]く｜待[ま]たなくて｜済[す]みます。

synonyms.note: ずに済む carries the identical meaning in a more formal, written register.

antonyms.note: ずには済まない means you won't be able to get away without doing it; なくて済む means you are spared from having to.

related.note: なくてもいい grants permission not to do; なくて済む reports that circumstances happily removed the need.

title: なくはない・なくもない
kana: なくはない・なくもない
romaji: naku wa nai / naku mo nai
meaning: it's not that ... isn't; ... to some degree (understated affirmation)
summary: 〜なくはない・〜なくもない is a reserved, hedged affirmation built from a double negative: 'it's not that there isn't ~', hence 'well, somewhat / I guess so'. 興味がなくはない = 'it's not that I have no interest'. The two negatives cancel into a mild, reluctant yes — weaker and more cautious than a plain affirmative.
structure: Verb［ない form → なく］＋は／も＋ない
pitfalls: It voices partial, grudging agreement, noticeably weaker than a direct affirmative.
The tone is reserved or hesitant; overusing it can sound evasive.

examples.ja: その提案に興味がなくはないが、もう少し詳しい説明がほしい。
examples.en: It's not that I have no interest in the proposal, but I'd like a bit more detail.
examples.f: その｜提案[ていあん]に｜興味[きょうみ]がなくはないが、もう｜少[すこ]し｜詳[くわ]しい｜説明[せつめい]がほしい。

examples.ja: 彼の言い分も、分からなくもない。
examples.en: I can sort of see his point of view, actually.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]の｜言い分[いいぶん]も、｜分[わ]からなくもない。

synonyms.note: ないでもない is the same understated 'it's not that ... not', with the same reluctant nuance.

related.note: ないことはない leans toward 'it's not impossible / there is a way'; なくはない is more about a faint degree of feeling or agreement.
ないものでもない means 'it's not entirely out of the question'; both hedge, with ものでもない sounding more literary.

title: 何から何まで
meaning: everything; each and every thing; from A to Z
summary: 何から何まで is a set phrase meaning 'absolutely everything, down to every detail'. The words are fixed and don't vary. It stresses the full extent of something — often in gratitude (何から何までお世話になりました) but also in complaint. It functions adverbially before the verb or as a predicate.
pitfalls: It is a fixed idiom; the two 何 do not change, and you cannot swap in other words.
It emphasizes exhaustive totality ('every single thing'), positive or negative depending on context.

examples.ja: 引っ越しのときは、何から何まで友人が手伝ってくれた。
examples.en: When I moved, my friend helped me with every single thing.
examples.f: ｜引っ越[ひっこ]しのときは、｜何[なに]から｜何[なに]まで｜友人[ゆうじん]が｜手伝[てつだ]ってくれた。

examples.ja: この旅館は、何から何まで行き届いたサービスで感心した。
examples.en: This inn impressed me with service so attentive it covered every last detail.
examples.f: この｜旅館[りょかん]は、｜何[なに]から｜何[なに]まで｜行き届[いきとど]いたサービスで｜感心[かんしん]した。

synonyms.note: ことごとく means 'every one without exception' in a more formal, written tone; 何から何まで is a set colloquial phrase for 'the whole lot'.

related.note: に至るまで stresses that the range extends even to an extreme point; 何から何まで simply asserts 'all of it, every part'.

title: 何しろ
meaning: after all; the thing is; at any rate
summary: 何しろ flags the reason or circumstance the speaker most wants to stress, often to explain or excuse — 'after all, the fact is ~'. It typically introduces a striking cause and pairs with a reason ending like ので/から/し. The nuance is 'given this key fact, no wonder', drawing the listener's attention to the decisive point.
pitfalls: It highlights the key reason or background; it usually leads into or sits beside a reason clause (ので／から／し).
It is fairly conversational; in stiff written explanations 何しろ can sound too casual.

examples.ja: 何しろ初めての経験だったので、緊張してうまく話せなかった。
examples.en: After all, it was my first time, so I got nervous and couldn't speak well.
examples.f: ｜何[なに]しろ｜初[はじ]めての｜経験[けいけん]だったので、｜緊張[きんちょう]してうまく｜話[はな]せなかった。

examples.ja: あの店はいつも混んでいる。何しろ味がいいからね。
examples.en: That place is always packed. Well, the food is good, after all.
examples.f: あの｜店[みせ]はいつも｜混[こ]んでいる。｜何[なに]しろ｜味[あじ]がいいからね。

synonyms.note: 何といっても singles out the most important point; 何しろ stresses a decisive reason or circumstance behind something.

title: 何も〜ない
meaning: nothing (at all); no need to go so far as to ~
summary: 何も with a negative predicate has two uses. Plainly it means 'nothing / not anything at all' — 何も残っていない = 'nothing is left'. Emphatically, 何も〜ことはない / 〜なくてもいい means 'there's no need to go so far as to ~', pushing back on an overreaction: 何もそこまで怒ることはない = 'no need to get that angry'.
structure: 何も ＋ Verb［plain］＋ことはない ［no need to go so far as］
pitfalls: 何も requires a negative predicate to follow; on its own it is not an affirmative 'anything'.
Distinguish the 'no need to' use (何も〜ことはない) from the plain 'nothing' use; the former argues an action is excessive, not literally absent.

examples.ja: 何もそんなに怒ることはないでしょう。ただの冗談ですよ。
examples.en: There's no need to get so worked up — it was just a joke.
examples.f: ｜何[なに]もそんなに｜怒[おこ]ることはないでしょう。ただの｜冗談[じょうだん]ですよ。

examples.ja: 冷蔵庫の中には、もう何も残っていなかった。
examples.en: There was nothing left at all in the fridge.
examples.f: ｜冷蔵庫[れいぞうこ]の｜中[なか]には、もう｜何[なに]も｜残[のこ]っていなかった。

related.note: 別に〜ない softens to 'not particularly'; 何も〜ない is a stronger 'nothing / not anything at all'.
ことはない alone says 'there's no need to'; 何も〜ことはない adds emphasis that going that far is uncalled for.

title: なにやら
meaning: something or other; some kind of; somehow
summary: なにやら points vaguely at an unspecified something the speaker can't (or won't) pin down — なにやら物音がする = 'there's some sort of noise'. It can also mean 'somehow, for some reason' about an indistinct impression. Slightly literary and atmospheric, it often carries a mysterious or uncertain nuance.
pitfalls: It is vaguer and more literary than なにか, often with a mysterious or indistinct feel.
It refers to something unidentified, not a clear choice among known options.

examples.ja: 隣の部屋で、なにやら物音がする。
examples.en: There's some sort of noise coming from the next room.
examples.f: ｜隣[となり]の｜部屋[へや]で、なにやら｜物音[ものおと]がする。

examples.ja: 彼はなにやら考え込んでいる様子だった。
examples.en: He looked to be brooding over something or other.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]はなにやら｜考え込[かんがえこ]んでいる｜様子[ようす]だった。

related.note: どうやら means 'apparently / it seems' (an inference); なにやら points at an unidentified thing or vague impression.

title: 何より
meaning: above all; more than anything; best of all
summary: 何より(も) means 'more than anything else', marking what is most important or valued — 健康が何より大切だ = 'health matters above all'. As the set phrase 〜が何よりだ, it expresses relief or gladness that nothing could be better: ご無事で何よりです = 'I'm so glad you're safe'.
structure: 何より（も） ＋ predicate ［above all else］
〜（て／で）何よりだ ［nothing could be better; so glad］
pitfalls: 何より(も) as an adverb means 'above all'; 何よりだ as a set phrase expresses relief or gladness.
It ranks one thing highest; it is not a general 'especially' scattered across many items.

examples.ja: 健康が何より大切だと、年をとって実感するようになった。
examples.en: As I've grown older, I've come to truly feel that health matters above all.
examples.f: ｜健康[けんこう]が｜何[なに]より｜大切[たいせつ]だと、｜年[とし]をとって｜実感[じっかん]するようになった。

examples.ja: ご無事で何よりです。
examples.en: I'm so glad you're safe — nothing could be better.
examples.f: ご｜無事[ぶじ]で｜何[なに]よりです。

synonyms.note: 何といっても also singles out the top point 'after all'; 何より more plainly ranks one thing as most important or best.

related.note: 一番 is the everyday superlative 'the most / number one'; 何より is a more emphatic 'more than anything else'.

title: ならともかく
meaning: if it were ~, that'd be one thing, but ~
summary: 〜ならともかく sets aside one case as understandable or excusable in order to contrast it with the actual case, which is not. 子供ならともかく = 'if it were a child it'd be one thing, but...'. The ならともかく clause names the acceptable hypothetical; the main clause states the real, often problematic situation, frequently with a critical tone.
pitfalls: The ならともかく part is the case you'd accept or excuse; the main clause is the actual case being criticized.
It usually carries a note of complaint or disapproval toward the real situation.

examples.ja: 子供ならともかく、大人がそんなことで泣くなんて情けない。
examples.en: If it were a child it'd be one thing, but for a grown-up to cry over something like that is pathetic.
examples.f: ｜子供[こども]ならともかく、｜大人[おとな]がそんなことで｜泣[な]くなんて｜情[なさ]けない。

examples.ja: 一度きりならともかく、毎回遅刻するのは問題だ。
examples.en: Once would be one thing, but showing up late every single time is a problem.
examples.f: ｜一[いち]｜度[ど]きりならともかく、｜毎回[まいかい]｜遅刻[ちこく]するのは｜問題[もんだい]だ。

synonyms.note: ならまだしも is very close ('if ~ then maybe, but'); both concede one case, with まだしも stressing 'still tolerable'.
はともかく simply sets a topic aside ('leaving ~ aside'); ならともかく contrasts a hypothetical acceptable case with the real one.

title: 何といっても
meaning: after all; more than anything; no matter what anyone says
summary: 何といっても singles out the one point the speaker considers most important or undeniable — 'when all's said and done, ~'. It introduces the standout reason, feature, or attraction: この町の魅力は何といっても〜 = 'the appeal of this town is, above all, ~'. The tone is confident, presenting the point as beyond dispute.
structure: 何といっても ＋ Sentence ［the single most important point］
pitfalls: It picks out the strongest single point, more emphatic than a plain 'especially'.
The following statement is presented as undeniable; it doesn't merely list one example among equals.

examples.ja: この町の魅力は、何といっても新鮮な海の幸だ。
examples.en: The appeal of this town is, more than anything, its fresh seafood.
examples.f: この｜町[まち]の｜魅力[みりょく]は、｜何[なに]といっても｜新鮮[しんせん]な｜海[うみ]の｜幸[こう]だ。

examples.ja: 夏の楽しみは、何といっても花火大会です。
examples.en: The best part of summer is, without a doubt, the fireworks festival.
examples.f: ｜夏[なつ]の｜楽[たの]しみは、｜何[なに]といっても｜花火[はなび]｜大会[たいかい]です。

synonyms.note: 何より ranks one thing highest 'above all'; 何といっても frames it as the undeniable point 'no matter what you say'.
何しろ stresses a decisive reason; 何といっても singles out the most important feature or point.

title: に値する
meaning: to be worth ~; to deserve ~
summary: 〜に値する means something is worthy of or deserves ~ (praise, attention, trust, consideration). 評価に値する = 'deserves recognition'. It attaches to a noun or a dictionary-form verb (注目するに値する) and belongs to formal or written Japanese, often in evaluation and commentary.
pitfalls: It takes a noun or a dictionary-form verb (信頼するに値する), not a た-form or ます-stem.
It is formal and written; in casual speech people say 〜の価値がある instead.

examples.ja: 彼の長年の努力は、高く評価されるに値する。
examples.en: His years of effort deserve high praise.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]の｜長年[ながねん]の｜努力[どりょく]は、｜高[たか]く｜評価[ひょうか]されるに｜値[あたい]する。

examples.ja: この研究は、専門家が注目するに値する成果だ。
examples.en: This research is an achievement worthy of the experts' attention.
examples.f: この｜研究[けんきゅう]は、｜専門[せんもん]｜家[か]が｜注目[ちゅうもく]するに｜値[あたい]する｜成果[せいか]だ。

synonyms.note: に足る also means 'worthy enough to' and is likewise formal, common in 信頼に足る; に値する emphasizes deserving in worth or merit.

antonyms.note: に足らない・に足りない means 'not worth ~ / too trivial to', the direct opposite of being worthy.

title: にあたって・にあたり
kana: にあたって・にあたり
meaning: on the occasion of; at the time of (undertaking)
summary: 〜にあたって・〜にあたり marks a significant moment — usually the start of an important undertaking — as the occasion for appropriate action. 開会にあたり = 'on the occasion of opening'. It is formal and forward-looking, used for milestones and ceremonies rather than everyday events. にあたって and にあたり are interchangeable, the latter a touch more formal.
structure: Verb［dictionary form］＋にあたって／にあたり
pitfalls: It suits significant, often formal occasions and the action taken for them; it isn't used for trivial daily events.
にあたって (て form) and にあたり (stem) mean the same thing; にあたり sounds slightly more formal and written.

examples.ja: 新規事業を始めるにあたって、まず市場を十分に調査した。
examples.en: In launching the new business, we first researched the market thoroughly.
examples.f: ｜新規[しんき]｜事業[じぎょう]を｜始[はじ]めるにあたって、まず｜市場[しじょう]を｜十分[じゅうぶん]に｜調査[ちょうさ]した。

examples.ja: 卒業にあたり、お世話になった先生に感謝の言葉を述べた。
examples.en: On the occasion of graduation, I expressed my thanks to the teachers who had helped me.
examples.f: ｜卒業[そつぎょう]にあたり、お｜世話[せわ]になった｜先生[せんせい]に｜感謝[かんしゃ]の｜言葉[ことば]を｜述[の]べた。

synonyms.note: に際して is very close ('on the occasion of'); にあたって leans toward preparing to undertake something, 際して toward a special moment or event.
に先立ち means 'prior to / in advance of', stressing timing before the event; にあたって marks the occasion itself.

related.note: 上で is a more procedural 'in the course of / when doing'; にあたって singles out an important occasion.

title: に応じて
meaning: depending on; in accordance with; to match ~
summary: 〜に応じて means something varies flexibly in response to a changing condition — the result adjusts to fit it. 収入に応じて = 'according to income'. It attaches to nouns, and 〜に応じた modifies a following noun (要望に応じたプラン). The nuance is adaptation: as the condition changes, the outcome changes with it.
pitfalls: It implies flexible adjustment to a variable condition, with the outcome shifting to match it.
Use 〜に応じた (not 〜に応じて) when modifying a noun: 状況に応じた対応.

examples.ja: 収入に応じて、税金の額が変わります。
examples.en: The amount of tax changes according to your income.
examples.f: ｜収入[しゅうにゅう]に｜応[おう]じて、｜税金[ぜいきん]の｜額[がく]が｜変[か]わります。

examples.ja: お客様のご要望に応じて、プランを自由に選べます。
examples.en: You can freely choose a plan to match the customer's requests.
examples.f: お｜客様[きゃくさま]のご｜要望[ようぼう]に｜応[おう]じて、プランを｜自由[じゆう]に｜選[えら]べます。

synonyms.note: に従って means 'in accordance with / as ~ proceeds'; に応じて stresses flexibly adapting the result to a variable.
次第で means the outcome hinges on ~ ('depending on'); に応じて stresses proportional adjustment to the condition.

related.note: によって covers 'depending on / by means of / due to' broadly; に応じて specifically means adapting flexibly to fit.

title: にかかわらず
meaning: regardless of; whether or not; irrespective of
summary: 〜にかかわらず means a result holds no matter which of the possibilities applies. It attaches to a noun (天候にかかわらず) or to a paired affirmative-and-negative (参加するしないにかかわらず, 有無にかかわらず). The point is that variation in the condition makes no difference to the outcome.
structure: Verb／い-adjective［affirmative + negative pair］＋にかかわらず
pitfalls: にかかわらず ('regardless of') is not にもかかわらず ('despite the fact that'); the latter concedes a real, established fact.
It often pairs opposite options — 行く行かず, 好き嫌い, 大小 — meaning the result is the same either way.

examples.ja: 天候にかかわらず、大会は予定どおり行われます。
examples.en: Regardless of the weather, the tournament will be held as scheduled.
examples.f: ｜天候[てんこう]にかかわらず、｜大会[たいかい]は｜予定[よてい]どおり｜行[おこな]われます。

examples.ja: 経験の有無にかかわらず、どなたでも応募できます。
examples.en: Anyone may apply, whether or not they have experience.
examples.f: ｜経験[けいけん]の｜有無[うむ]にかかわらず、どなたでも｜応募[おうぼ]できます。

synonyms.note: を問わず also means 'regardless of / irrespective of'; both are formal, with を問わず common in notices (年齢を問わず).

related.note: にもかかわらず means 'despite', conceding a real fact; にかかわらず means 'no matter which', with no fact conceded.
によらず likewise means 'regardless of / not depending on'; にかかわらず often pairs opposite options for 'either way'.

title: に関わる
meaning: to concern; to affect; to have a serious bearing on
summary: 〜に関わる means to have a weighty bearing on something important — life, honor, credibility, a future. 命に関わる = 'a matter of life and death'; 信用に関わる問題 = 'an issue that affects one's credibility'. It implies serious stakes, not a casual 'about', and often modifies the noun that follows.
pitfalls: It implies a serious, high-stakes bearing (命・名誉・信用); for the neutral 'concerning / about', use に関して or について.
Don't confuse it with にかかわらず ('regardless of'), which shares the 関わ root but has the opposite grammatical role.

examples.ja: これは会社の信用に関わる重大な問題です。
examples.en: This is a grave matter that affects the company's credibility.
examples.f: これは｜会社[かいしゃ]の｜信用[しんよう]に｜関[かか]わる｜重大[じゅうだい]な｜問題[もんだい]です。

examples.ja: 少しの油断が命に関わることもある。
examples.en: A moment's carelessness can be a matter of life and death.
examples.f: ｜少[すこ]しの｜油断[ゆだん]が｜命[いのち]に｜関[かか]わることもある。

related.note: に関して・に関する is the neutral 'concerning / about (a topic)'; に関わる implies a serious, high-stakes bearing.
について is a plain 'about ~'; に関わる means something critically affects the matter, not merely relates to it.
にかかわらず ('regardless of') shares the 関わ root but flips the grammar to 'no matter ~', not 'affects ~'.

title: に限って
meaning: of all things/times; (that person) especially would not ~
summary: Noun＋に限って singles out one specific noun with a nuance of irony or exception. With a following negative it defends a particular person or thing — うちの子に限ってそんなことはしない ('my child of all people would never do that'). With an event or time it complains that bad luck strikes at exactly the wrong moment — 急いでいる時に限って ('of all times, just when I'm in a hurry').
pitfalls: Two flavors: with a negative it defends a specific person or thing (あの人に限って…ない); with a time or event it grumbles that bad timing lines up (…時に限って).
Same 限 root as に限る ('is best') and に限らず ('not only'), but the meanings are different — don't blur them together.

examples.ja: 彼女に限って、そんな大事な約束を忘れるはずがありません。
examples.en: She of all people would never forget such an important promise.
examples.f: ｜彼女[かのじょ]に｜限[かぎ]って、そんな｜大事[だいじ]な｜約束[やくそく]を｜忘[わす]れるはずがありません。

examples.ja: 急いでいる時に限って、なかなかタクシーが来ない。
examples.en: It's exactly when I'm in a hurry that a taxi just won't come.
examples.f: ｜急[いそ]いでいる｜時[とき]に｜限[かぎ]って、なかなかタクシーが｜来[こ]ない。

antonyms.note: に限らず broadens ('not only N'); に限って narrows in on one specific N — opposite directions from the same 限.

related.note: に限る recommends N as the best choice; に限って singles N out with an ironic or defensive nuance.

title: に限らず
meaning: not limited to; not just ~ but also
summary: Noun＋に限らず says the statement is 'not limited to' the named noun but reaches more widely — 週末に限らず平日も ('not just on weekends but on weekdays too'). It broadens the scope beyond the single case, and usually a following 〜も／〜まで names the wider group it extends to.
pitfalls: Normally paired with a following 〜も or 〜まで that names the broader group the statement extends to.
に限らず broadens the scope ('not only N'); に限って narrows onto one specific N — the same 限 pulling opposite ways.

examples.ja: この公園は週末に限らず、平日もたくさんの人でにぎわっている。
examples.en: This park is crowded not just on weekends but on weekdays too.
examples.f: この｜公園[こうえん]は｜週末[しゅうまつ]に｜限[かぎ]らず、｜平日[へいじつ]もたくさんの｜人[ひと]でにぎわっている。

examples.ja: 最近は若者に限らず、幅広い世代がこのアプリを使っている。
examples.en: Lately it's not only young people — a wide range of generations use this app.
examples.f: ｜最近[さいきん]は｜若者[わかもの]に｜限[かぎ]らず、｜幅広[はばひろ]い｜世代[せだい]がこのアプリを｜使[つか]っている。

synonyms.note: のみならず also means 'not only ~ but also', in a more literary register; に限らず is a shade plainer.
だけでなく is the everyday 'not only ~ but also'; に限らず is slightly more formal and attaches straight to a noun.

antonyms.note: に限って singles out one specific N; に限らず insists the point is not limited to that N.

related.note: はもちろん takes the first item as obvious and adds more; に限らず simply denies that the scope stops at one item.

title: にかけては
meaning: when it comes to (a skill someone excels at)
summary: Noun＋にかけては singles out a field or skill and claims that, in that area, someone is second to none — 料理にかけては彼の右に出る者はいない ('when it comes to cooking, no one beats him'). The clause that follows almost always asserts excellence or confidence.
pitfalls: The following clause is normally positive — a claim of being the best or most confident; it does not fit neutral or negative statements.
Don't confuse it with にかけて ('from A over to B / spanning a range'); にかけては marks a domain of expertise.

examples.ja: 記憶力にかけては、クラスの誰にも負けない自信があります。
examples.en: When it comes to memory, I'm confident I won't lose to anyone in the class.
examples.f: ｜記憶[きおく]｜力[りょく]にかけては、クラスの｜誰[だれ]にも｜負[ま]けない｜自信[じしん]があります。

examples.ja: 速さにかけては、この選手が世界でトップだと言われている。
examples.en: When it comes to speed, this athlete is said to be the best in the world.
examples.f: ｜速[はや]さにかけては、この｜選手[せんしゅ]が｜世界[せかい]でトップだと｜言[い]われている。
